name: Jersey finger (FDP avulsion)
populations: people who catch a flexed finger on clothing or equipment
summary: Avulsion of the FDP tendon from the distal phalanx when a flexed fingertip is forced into extension, most often in the ring finger. The tendon can retract into the palm, so early surgical review is essential.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Surgical reinsertion, then protected motion. In 29 operated patients, 12 had excellent or good Buck-Gramcko results and 10 had poor results

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Cannot actively flex the DIP joint when the PIP joint is held (FDP test), while PIP flexion is preserved by the FDS

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiograph for a bony avulsion; ultrasound or MRI for a purely tendinous avulsion

keyFacts.label: Digit
keyFacts.value: Ring finger in about 80% of cases in one report; 16 ring and 13 little fingers among 32 operated patients in a series

keyFacts.label: Timing
keyFacts.value: Mean interval from injury to surgery was 6.8 days (range 0–32) in that series

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Leddy and Packer types I–III by level of retraction; types IV and V add associated fractures

overview:
Jersey finger is avulsion of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon from its insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx. The most common mechanism is forceful hyperextension of an actively flexed distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint, as when a fingertip gripping an opponent's jersey is pulled away. It is seen most often in the ring finger because the FDP is tethered there by the lumbricals in the palm [r1]. The patient cannot actively flex the DIP joint when making a fist and has reduced pinch and grasp strength [r1]. It is an uncommon injury in surgical series [r2], and in athletes it is easily mistaken for a sprain or goes unreported [r3].

The classification of Leddy and Packer is based on the level of tendon retraction and the state of the vincula. It determines how urgent repair is and how likely it is to succeed [r1]. Acute injuries are usually treated operatively, and the results of repair are time-dependent [r1,r4]. In a series of 32 operated patients the mean time from injury to surgery was 6.8 days, and quick diagnosis and surgery were linked with restoration of full range of motion [r2]. The evidence base is case reports and retrospective series. Randomised evidence for postoperative rehabilitation is lacking and very low certainty [r5].

epidemiology.text:
Jersey finger is seen in contact sports such as rugby and football [r1], and in American football and basketball [r6]. One report described it as primarily affecting the ring finger (in 80% of cases) and described two cases in professional soccer players, which raised the question of whether its epidemiology is changing as rugby injury rates fall with better equipment. Population incidence figures were not retrieved from the sources used for this page, so none are quoted [r7].

In a French series of 32 operated patients, 26 were male, the mean age was 37.2 years (range 16–68), 11 injuries were sports injuries, 16 involved the ring finger and 13 the little finger [r2]. Non-sporting mechanisms are reported: rising from a chair [r1] and restraining a dog by its collar [r8].

intrinsic: Ring finger anatomy: the FDP is tethered by the lumbricals in the palm, which makes the ring finger most susceptible [r1]
Male sex: 26 of 32 operated patients in one series were men (descriptive, not a risk estimate) [r2]
Young to middle adulthood: mean age 37.2 years in the same series [r2]
extrinsic: Contact sports in which players grip an opponent's jersey, such as rugby, football and basketball [r1,r6]
Tackling and grappling activities, including martial arts (case report) [r3]
Gripping an object that is suddenly pulled away, for example a dog collar [r8]
Jersey design and refereeing rules, which one author suggested may need to change [r7]

mechanism.summary: The finger is flexed and gripping when an outside force pulls the fingertip into extension. This is a forceful hyperextension of an actively flexed DIP joint, so the FDP is loaded eccentrically while it is contracting [r1,r6]. The tendon is avulsed from the volar base of the distal phalanx, with or without a bone fragment [r1]. A computational model of a gripped rod pulled away at sprinting speed produced avulsion at high levels of muscle activation (80% and above) [r6].
sequence: The athlete grips an opponent's jersey or equipment with the fingers flexed and the FDP contracting [r1].
The opponent pulls away, and the gripped fingertip is forced into extension against the active flexion [r1,r6].
The FDP is loaded eccentrically beyond its capacity. In the ring finger the tethering effect of the lumbricals adds to the load [r1].
The tendon avulses from the volar base of the distal phalanx, either alone or with a bony fragment [r1].
The tendon retracts, and the level depends on the vincula and on whether a bony fragment catches on the A4 pulley (palm, PIP level or A4 level) [r1].

The athlete feels a pop and pain at the fingertip or palm, and cannot flex the DIP joint. Pain often settles over a few weeks, which leaves only an inability to make a full fist (a general statement in a case report [r1]).
An undiagnosed injury can be missed as a sprain, and good results are time-dependent [r3,r4].

variants.name: Tendon-only avulsion (Leddy and Packer types I and II)
variants.description: The tendon pulls off without bone, and retracts to the palm (type I) or to the PIP level (type II) [r1].

variants.name: Bony avulsion (type III)
variants.description: A large bony fragment is avulsed and is held at the level of the A4 pulley [r1].

variants.name: Fracture combined with tendon avulsion (type IV)
variants.description: A fracture of the volar base of the distal phalanx coexists with avulsion of the FDP, with the tendon separated from the fragment. Definitions vary between sources [r9,r4,r1].

variants.name: Avulsion with a separate fracture (type V)
variants.description: FDP avulsion with an extra-articular (Va) or intra-articular (Vb) fracture, a proposal that extended the classification [r1].

variants.name: Combined FDP and FDS avulsion (double jersey finger)
variants.description: A rare pattern that complicates surgery and prognosis. A review of 24 cases highlighted micro-anchor repair and early active mobilisation [r10].

variants.name: Non-sporting and unusual mechanisms
variants.description: Reported after rising from a chair and after restraining a dog by its collar, where a large extra-articular fragment was avulsed [r1,r8].

anatomy.text: The FDP tendon flexes the DIP joint and inserts on the volar base of the distal phalanx. In the finger it runs in the flexor sheath, deep to the FDS, and its blood supply arrives through the vincula (long and short), which tether it to the phalanges (clinical anatomy). The A4 pulley lies over the middle phalanx and can stop a bony fragment from retracting further [r1]. The FDS inserts on the middle phalanx, so PIP flexion is preserved after an FDP avulsion and the patient loses only DIP flexion [r1]. The lumbricals arise from the FDP tendons in the palm, and this tethering is the explanation given for the ring finger's susceptibility [r1].

structures.name: FDP tendon
structures.role: The only flexor of the DIP joint. It avulses from the volar base of the distal phalanx in jersey finger [r1].

structures.name: Long and short vincula
structures.role: Carry the blood supply to the FDP. The state of the vincula after injury helps determine the outcome of repair [r1].

structures.name: A4 pulley (and A2 pulley)
structures.role: Annular pulleys over the middle and proximal phalanges. A bony fragment can be held at the A4 level [r1].

structures.name: FDS tendon
structures.role: Inserts on the middle phalanx and preserves PIP flexion when the FDP is avulsed [r1]

structures.name: Lumbricals
structures.role: Arise from the FDP in the palm and tether the tendon, particularly in the ring finger [r1]

structures.name: Volar base of the distal phalanx
structures.role: The FDP insertion and the site of avulsion fragments [r1]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In jersey finger the FDP tendon is avulsed at its bony insertion. The consequences depend on where it retracts. When the tendon retracts into the palm, both vincula rupture and its blood supply is compromised (type I). When it stops at the PIP level, the long vinculum is spared and the blood supply is preserved (type II). When a bony fragment is attached, the fragment is held at the A4 pulley (type III) [r1]. The level of retraction and the status of the long and short vincula determine the outcome of repair [r1].

Because an avulsed tendon retracts and the muscle shortens, delayed repair can require tendon grafting, and chronic injuries are managed according to the patient's need for DIP function. Some asymptomatic patients with a chronic ring finger injury can be left alone, because the intact FDS preserves PIP flexion [r1]. In a finite-element model of a gripped rod pulled from the hand, avulsions occurred at high muscle activation, with no tendon strain injuries elsewhere [r6].

structures.name: FDP tendon
structures.effect: Avulsed from the distal phalanx, and retracts to the A4, PIP or palm level [r1]

structures.name: Vincula
structures.effect: Ruptured in type I and spared (long vinculum) in type II [r1]

structures.name: Distal phalanx volar base
structures.effect: A bony fragment may avulse with the tendon (types III–V) [r1,r9]

structures.name: A4 pulley
structures.effect: Can arrest a retracting bony fragment [r1]

structures.name: DIP joint
structures.effect: Intra-articular fractures are described in type V injuries, and persistent instability may need DIP arthrodesis in chronic cases [r1]

muscles.name: FDP muscle
muscles.effect: Loses its distal attachment, retracts and shortens, and the longer the delay the harder it is to bring the tendon back to bone (clinical).

muscles.name: FDS
muscles.effect: Stays intact and preserves PIP flexion, which can mask the diagnosis [r1].

muscles.name: Lumbricals and intrinsics
muscles.effect: Tether the retracted FDP in the palm and can be tender at the stump (clinical).

cellular.description: Bleeding and inflammatory cells at the avulsion site and along the sheath (typical tendon-healing timeline; clinical).
After repair, fibroblasts bridge the tendon-bone junction. Adhesions in the sheath are the main early risk, which is why controlled early motion is used [r11].
Collagen aligns along the line of load and the repair gains strength gradually (clinical).
The stump remains retracted and pain settles, leaving a lost DIP flexion that can be accepted, grafted or arthrodesed depending on need [r1].

systems.effect: Acute pain at the fingertip or palm often settles over a few weeks, leaving the loss of DIP flexion as the main problem (a general statement in a case report [r1]).
Vincula rupture in a type I injury compromises tendon blood supply, which affects healing after repair [r1].
Loss of DIP flexion weakens pinch and grasp [r1]. Nearby fractures can mask the injury, as in a rugby player whose FDP avulsion was found 4 weeks after a middle phalanx fracture [r12].
Athletes may under-report or delay care because of in-season play, so diagnosis can be late [r3,r13].

grading.system: Leddy and Packer classification (types I–III), with later additions (types IV and V)

grades.description: The FDP tendon retracts into the palm, and both vincula rupture, which compromises its blood supply [r1].
grades.prognosis: Needs the most urgent repair because retraction and loss of blood supply threaten the outcome (clinical reasoning from [r1]). In one series, 16 of 32 injuries were type I [r2].

grades.description: The FDP tendon retracts to the level of the PIP joint, and the long vinculum is spared, so the blood supply is preserved [r1].
grades.prognosis: 4 of 32 operated injuries in one series were type II [r2]

grades.description: The FDP tendon is avulsed with a bony fragment, which stops at the level of the A4 pulley [r1].
grades.prognosis: 5 of 32 operated injuries in one series were type III [r2]

grades.description: A fracture of the volar distal phalanx combined with FDP avulsion, with the tendon separated from the bony fragment as described by Smith. Buscemi and Page proposed adding it as a type IV injury (FDP avulsion with a concomitant, separate intra-articular fracture), so definitions vary between sources [r1,r4,r9].
grades.prognosis: 7 of 32 operated injuries in one series were type IV [r2]

grades.description: FDP avulsion with a separate fracture of the distal phalanx, extra-articular (Va) or intra-articular (Vb) [r1].
grades.prognosis: Rare; reported mainly as case reports and often needs fixation of the fragment [r1]

timeframes.summary: The biggest time variable is the delay between injury and repair, because results are time-dependent [r4]. In a series of 32 operated patients, the mean interval from injury to surgery was 6.8 days (range 0–32) [r2]. The healing phases below are an illustrative tendon-healing model, and postoperative timings are common clinical conventions because no trial defines them [r5].

healing.description: Pain and swelling; early recognition and surgical referral are essential [r3,r2]
Repair is protected while controlled motion limits adhesions (clinical convention; [r11])
Progression from active to light resisted motion per surgeon protocol (clinical)
Gradual build of grip strength and return to contact sport with clearance (clinical)

milestones.label: Diagnosis and surgical referral
milestones.note: Quick diagnosis and surgery were linked with full range of motion in a series of 32 patients [r2]

milestones.label: Surgery (series mean)
milestones.note: Mean interval from injury to surgery 6.8 days (range 0–32) [r2]

milestones.label: Wires out and active extension (one case)
milestones.note: In a case report, K-wires were removed at 3 weeks, followed by active extension and passive flexion of the DIP joint [r1]

milestones.label: Pinch and grasp loading (one case)
milestones.note: In the same case report pinch and grasp were allowed at about 6 weeks after surgery as strength improved [r1]

milestones.label: Return to play, individualised
milestones.note: Return to play depends on the patient, the sport and the timing of the injury [r14]

timeframes.returnToSport: Return to play is individualised by the patient, the sport and the timing of injury [r14]. It is criteria-based: a healed repair cleared by the surgeon, a full composite fist, near-normal grip and no pain on gripping. Typical timing after repair is about 3 months for contact sport (a common clinical convention), and no controlled data were found.

symptoms: A pop or tearing sensation at the fingertip after a finger was pulled out of a grip
Pain at the fingertip and sometimes in the palm over the retracted tendon
Inability to bend the tip of the finger, often noticed only when making a fist
Pain that often settles over a few weeks while the deficit remains [r1]
signs: The DIP joint stays extended when the patient makes a fist [r1]
Passive DIP flexion is full, although active DIP flexion is absent [r1]
PIP and MCP flexion are preserved because the FDS and intrinsics are intact [r1]
Swelling and tenderness on the volar finger, which may mark the level of retraction [r1]
A lump in the palm or at the PIP level where the stump has retracted (clinical)

subjective: Mechanism: a gripped finger pulled away, as in a tackle, or an unusual household pull [r1,r8]
Whether the athlete felt a pop, and whether the finger can bend at the tip
Time since injury, because delay narrows the options [r4]
Sport, position, season timing and hand dominance [r3,r14]
Previous finger injuries, and any other injury in the same finger [r12]
observation: Finger cascade: the affected finger stays extended at the DIP joint when the others flex [r1]
Swelling or bruising of the volar finger
palpation: Tenderness along the flexor sheath and the point of the retracted stump, which may suggest the retraction level [r1]
Palm for a lump over the lumbrical origin
rangeOfMotion: Active and passive DIP flexion, comparing digits
strength: FDP test: hold the PIP joint extended and ask the patient to flex the DIP joint
FDS test: hold the other fingers extended and ask the patient to flex the PIP joint
neuro: Digital sensation on both sides of the finger
functional: Grip on a jersey, bar or racquet (sport-specific)
Ability to make a full fist

specialTests.name: FDP isolation test
specialTests.purpose: Detect loss of FDP function at the DIP joint
specialTests.procedure: Hold the middle phalanx and PIP joint of the finger still in extension. Ask the patient to bend the fingertip.
specialTests.positive: The patient cannot actively flex the DIP joint, although passive flexion is full [r1]. No sensitivity or specificity figures were found.

specialTests.name: FDS isolation test
specialTests.purpose: Show that FDS function and PIP flexion are intact, and help to avoid missing the FDP injury
specialTests.procedure: Hold the other fingers in full extension, which blocks the FDP. Ask the patient to flex the PIP joint of the injured finger.
specialTests.positive: PIP flexion is present, so the FDS is intact, while DIP flexion is absent (FDP avulsion pattern) [r1].

specialTests.name: Palpation for the retracted stump
specialTests.procedure: Palpate along the volar finger, the PIP level and the distal palm for tenderness or a lump.
specialTests.positive: Point tenderness along the FDP course may indicate the retraction level [r1].

clinicalRules.name: Test FDP function in every finger injury from a tackle
clinicalRules.description: Injuries can be misdiagnosed as sprains or unreported by athletes, and flexor tendon avulsions require prompt recognition and appropriate treatment to prevent permanent disability [r3]. A nearby fracture can mask the injury [r12].

outcomeMeasures.name: Buck-Gramcko score
outcomeMeasures.use: Functional grading used after surgery for jersey finger [r2]

outcomeMeasures.name: QuickDASH
outcomeMeasures.use: Upper-limb disability; mean 5.66 in an operated series [r2]

outcomeMeasures.name: Grip and pinch dynamometry
outcomeMeasures.use: Strength compared with the other hand [r1]

imaging.findings: A bony avulsion fragment from the volar distal phalanx, and its position along the finger [r1]

imaging.indication: Isolated tendon avulsion, to find the level of retraction
imaging.findings: Useful for isolated tendon ruptures [r1]. In one case ultrasound was inconclusive [r12].

imaging.indication: When the diagnosis is unclear or ultrasound is inconclusive
imaging.findings: Showed avulsion of the FDP from the distal phalanx in a case that ultrasound had not clarified [r12]

differentials.name: Mallet finger
differentials.distinguishing: The opposite deficit: forced flexion of an extended DIP joint, with loss of active DIP extension and a droopy tip. In jersey finger the tip cannot flex.

differentials.name: A2 pulley rupture
differentials.distinguishing: A crimp-grip injury with a pop at the proximal phalanx, bowstringing and pain over the pulley. DIP flexion is retained.

differentials.name: PIP volar plate injury
differentials.distinguishing: Hyperextension injury to the PIP joint with volar swelling and tenderness, and no loss of isolated DIP flexion.

differentials.name: Finger sprain (misdiagnosis)
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and swelling settle, but the DIP joint still cannot flex. A sprain does not remove active DIP flexion [r3].

differentials.name: Distal phalanx fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Crush or direct injury with tuft or shaft fracture on radiograph; FDP function is intact unless a volar-base fragment is avulsed [r1].

differentials.name: Combined FDP and FDS avulsion
differentials.distinguishing: Both PIP and DIP flexion are lost, and the finger lies extended; rare [r10].

differentials.name: Anterior interosseous nerve palsy
differentials.distinguishing: Loss of FDP to the index finger (with FPL) without trauma to the finger, with no local tenderness or swelling (clinical).

redFlags: Inability to flex the fingertip after a gripped finger was pulled away: suspect FDP avulsion and arrange urgent hand surgical review the same or next day. Retraction and delay compromise repair [r1,r4,r2].
A palmar or PIP-level lump with a finger that cannot flex at the DIP joint: the tendon may have retracted (type I or II). Do not wait for pain to settle [r1].
A fracture of the same finger, or a presumed sprain that still cannot flex the tip: re-examine FDP function, because the avulsion can be missed [r12,r3].
Presentation weeks after the injury with a lost DIP flexion: still refer. Options include leaving an asymptomatic finger alone, grafting or DIP arthrodesis [r1].
After surgery, a sudden loss of active flexion suggests repair rupture, and a hot, red, draining wound suggests infection. Arrange urgent surgical review (clinical).
An open wound or laceration over the finger is a flexor tendon laceration, not a closed avulsion, and needs emergency repair (clinical).

management.principles: Diagnose FDP loss early and refer for surgical review at once. Acute injuries are usually treated operatively, and the choice for chronic injuries depends on the patient's need for DIP function [r1]. Results are time-dependent [r4]. Reinsertion by suture anchor, pull-out technique or both restored a good range of motion in a series, with 12 of 29 evaluated patients rated excellent or good on the Buck-Gramcko score, and 10 rated poor [r2]. After surgery, controlled mobilisation protocols are widely used, but the Cochrane review found very low-certainty evidence, and no trials tested orthoses or the timing of starting mobilisation [r5]. The physio's key tasks are early recognition, urgent referral and graded rehabilitation under the surgeon's protocol [r3,r13].

medical.name: Early surgical reinsertion of the FDP (suture anchor or pull-out)
medical.description: Acute jersey finger is usually treated operatively [r1], and some authors regard it as treatable only by surgery [r4]. In 32 operated patients the mean interval from injury to surgery was 6.8 days, with anchor, pull-out or combined techniques. Of 29 evaluated, 6 had excellent, 6 good, 7 satisfactory and 10 poor results (Buck-Gramcko), the mean QuickDASH was 5.66, and 12 complications occurred in 9 patients [r2].

medical.name: Open reduction and fixation of a bony fragment (K-wires)
medical.description: Used when a large fragment is attached (types III–V). Case reports describe good outcomes with K-wire fixation [r1,r8]. Stabilising the DIP joint may be needed even at the cost of early motion in the rare combination injuries [r9].

medical.name: Anchor repair with early active mobilisation for double (FDP and FDS) avulsion
medical.description: A systematic review and case series of 24 cases highlighted micro suture anchors, which give strength and allow early mobilisation [r10].

medical.name: Delayed or chronic injury: observation, tendon graft or DIP arthrodesis
medical.description: An asymptomatic chronic ring finger injury can be left, because the intact FDS preserves PIP flexion. Patients needing fine DIP function can have tendon grafting, and persistent DIP instability may be treated by arthrodesis [r1].

medical.name: Nonoperative management of an acute avulsion
medical.description: Authors state acute jersey finger is usually treated operatively [r1] and that it can only be treated surgically [r4]. Splinting alone does not reattach the tendon (clinical reasoning).

medical.name: Analgesia
medical.description: Simple analgesia for the acute phase. No trial data were found for this injury.

physio.name: Early recognition and urgent referral
physio.description: Test FDP function in any finger injury from a tackle. Flexor tendon avulsions can be misdiagnosed as sprains or unreported, and need prompt recognition to avoid permanent disability [r3]. Assessment, treatment and return to play should be individualised [r14,r13].

physio.name: Controlled early mobilisation after repair
physio.description: In zone II repairs, early controlled mobilisation (passive or active) is the cornerstone of rehabilitation, depending on the strength of the repair and patient adherence [r11]. For flexor tendon repairs generally, a Cochrane review of 17 studies found only very low-certainty evidence, and no trials of orthoses or timing of starting mobilisation [r5]. Zone I (distal) injuries were not the focus of either review, so apply the surgeon's protocol.

physio.name: Active extension and passive flexion after pin removal (case-report protocol)
physio.description: In one case, wires were removed at 3 weeks and active extension with passive flexion of the DIP joint began, with pinch and grasp allowed from about 6 weeks as strength improved [r1].

physio.name: Scar management, oedema control and desensitisation
Early resisted gripping or forced passive extension of the repaired tendon
physio.description: Tendon ruptures were recorded in trials of mobilisation regimens after flexor tendon repair [r5]. Delay resisted loading until the surgeon allows it (clinical).

education: A finger that cannot bend at the tip after being pulled from a grip needs a surgeon's opinion urgently, even when the pain has gone.
The earlier the tendon is reattached, the better the result is likely to be [r4,r2].
Wear the splint as advised and do not grip or lift with the repaired finger until cleared.
Recovery takes weeks to months. Your therapist will progress movement carefully so the repair is not overloaded.
Avoid grabbing an opponent's jersey or equipment with hooked fingers once you return to sport (clinical).

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation follows the surgeon's protocol, which depends on the repair technique, the retraction type and any bony fixation. No trial has defined the best protocol for this injury, and a Cochrane review of flexor tendon repair rehabilitation found only very low-certainty evidence and no trials of orthoses or the timing of starting mobilisation [r5]. Early controlled mobilisation, passive or active according to repair strength and adherence, is the principle in zone II repairs [r11]. The stages below describe a typical sequence, and exercise dosages are common clinical conventions. In one case report K-wires came out at 3 weeks, with active extension and passive flexion after that, and pinch and grasp allowed from about 6 weeks [r1].

stages.name: Protect the repair
goals: Teach splint care and wound protection
precautions: No active DIP flexion or resisted gripping until the surgeon allows
No forced passive DIP extension against the repair
Check the wound and for infection; report sudden loss of flexion
Follow the surgeon's protocol for pins and splint [r1]

exercises.name: Splint wear and care
exercises.dosage: Continuously except for supervised hygiene, as directed by the surgeon
exercises.cues: Keep the finger in the protected position and avoid gripping

exercises.name: Active movement of uninvolved fingers, thumb and wrist
exercises.cues: Keep the rest of the hand moving

exercises.name: Gentle passive flexion within the splint (protocol-dependent)
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions, 4–6 times daily if the surgeon prescribes it (clinical convention; protocols vary [r5])
exercises.cues: Move the finger slowly with the other hand and release gently

exercises.name: Elevation and oedema control
exercises.dosage: Hand above the elbow when resting; light compression if advised (clinical)
exercises.cues: Active fist and release for uninvolved fingers

exercises.name: Shoulder and elbow range of motion

progressionCriteria: Wound healed and sutures out (2 weeks in one case report) [r1]
Surgeon clearance to begin active motion
No sign of infection or repair failure

stages.name: Protected active motion
goals: Begin active extension and controlled DIP flexion
precautions: Follow the surgeon's limits on active flexion
Stop if pain or swelling increases

exercises.name: Active DIP extension with the PIP supported
exercises.cues: Smooth, relaxed movement; stop if the repair is sore

exercises.name: Passive DIP flexion progressing to active-assisted (protocol-dependent)
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions, 4 times daily after wire removal (clinical convention; case report [r1])

exercises.name: Tendon glide sequence (hook, straight, full fist)
exercises.dosage: 5–10 repetitions, 3 times daily once the surgeon allows

exercises.name: Scar massage and desensitisation
exercises.dosage: 5 minutes, 3 times daily once the wound has healed

progressionCriteria: Active DIP flexion without pain or lag
No increase in swelling after exercise

stages.name: Restore motion & strength
goals: Return to daily and work tasks
Remove the splint during the day
precautions: Avoid sudden pulls or catching the fingertip on objects

exercises.name: Blocked DIP flexion
exercises.cues: Hold the middle phalanx still and flex only the tip

exercises.name: Soft putty grip, then pinch
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10 with 3–5 s holds, 3 times weekly, starting with the softest putty

exercises.name: Wrist flexion and extension with light load
Functional tasks (buttons, keys, jar opening)
exercises.cues: Use the whole hand without jerky pulling

progressionCriteria: Pinch and grip at least 70% of the other side (a common clinical convention)

stages.name: Return to sport & work
goals: Return to contact sport and heavy work
Restore grip strength near the other side
Protect the finger on early return
Teach safer handling of jerseys and equipment
precautions: Tape or protect the finger initially (clinical convention)
Avoid hooking fingers into clothing or equipment

exercises.name: Graded tool or bar gripping
exercises.dosage: Start at 50% of usual volume and add 10–20% a week (clinical convention)

progressionCriteria: Grip about 90% of the other side (a common clinical convention)
Full composite fist and pain-free gripping

criteria: Healed repair and clearance from the surgeon
Full or near-full composite fist and active DIP flexion
Grip and pinch about 90% of the other hand (a common clinical convention)
No pain or tenderness at the fingertip or palm with gripping
Plan to avoid hooking fingers into jerseys or equipment [r7]
Return individualised to the patient, sport and timing of injury [r14]
tests: Goniometric DIP flexion and tip-to-palm distance

prognosis: Results depend on the retraction level, the status of the vincula and the speed of repair [r1,r4]. In 29 evaluated patients (a mean of 36.6 months from surgery to discharge), 6 had excellent, 6 good, 7 satisfactory and 10 poor results on the Buck-Gramcko score, the mean QuickDASH was 5.66, and 12 complications occurred in 9 patients, with no infections. The authors concluded that rapid diagnosis and rapid surgery led to restoration of full range of motion [r2]. Chronic or unrepaired injuries can be tolerated by some patients [r1]. There are no comparative trials of treatments or rehabilitation protocols, so these figures come from a single retrospective series and case reports [r2,r5].
prevention: No trial has tested prevention. Avoid gripping an opponent's jersey with hooked fingers in contact sport (clinical advice).
One author suggested that jerseys and refereeing rules may need to change to reduce the injury [r7].
Teach athletes to report a fingertip that cannot bend after a tackle, so that diagnosis is early [r3].
Avoid wrapping or hooking a finger through a dog lead, collar or machinery handle that can be suddenly pulled away (clinical) [r8].
clinicalPearls: A finger that stays extended at the DIP joint in a fist after a tackle is a jersey finger until proven otherwise [r1].
Do not be reassured when the pain settles. It often settles over a few weeks, and the lost DIP flexion can be the only sign left [r1].
Think of the ring finger first (about 80% in one report), but the little finger was also common in an operated series (13 of 32) [r7,r2].
A nearby fracture can hide the avulsion. Re-test FDP function when a finger fracture is slow to recover [r12].
Palpate for point tenderness along the volar finger and palm, which may show the level of retraction [r1].
Refer early. Good results are time-dependent, and the mean time to surgery in the series was 6.8 days [r4,r2].

captions.text: A defender chases a ball carrier and reaches out to grab his jersey.
The fingers close on the jersey with the fingertips flexed and the flexor muscle contracting.
The ball carrier accelerates away and forcibly pulls the gripped fingertips into extension.
The tendon that bends the fingertip is torn from the bone.
Zooming into the gripping finger, seen from the side.

actions.text: FDP avulsed from the distal phalanx

captions.text: The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) inserts on the volar base of the distal phalanx.
A gripped fingertip is pulled into extension while the FDP is contracting.
The tendon is avulsed from its insertion, sometimes with a fragment of bone.
The stump retracts as far as the PIP joint (type II) or the palm (type I).
The intact FDS keeps PIP flexion, so only the tip cannot bend. Early surgical review is essential.
Healthy tendon: parallel, crimped type I collagen fibres.
An active flexor contraction loads the fibres as the finger grips.
The sudden extension force exceeds the tendon's capacity at its insertion.
The tendon fails, or pulls its bone fragment off the distal phalanx.
Torn vessels bleed, and the retracted tendon loses its blood supply if the vincula rupture.
Inflammatory cells clear debris over the first days.
After repair, fibroblasts bridge the tendon–bone junction, and early controlled motion limits adhesions.
Collagen remodels along the line of load. A repair gains strength slowly.
